feed.title: CyberBiota3
feed.subtitle: My open-source home lab, the services I run, and what I learn along the way.

entry.title: Giving the agents separate jobs

link.title: Giving the agents separate jobs

entry.content:
CyberBiota3 already had 14 agent IDs when I started this upgrade. The coordinator was connected to Telegram, and the older roles had existing workflows. Replacing their configuration in one step would have made it harder to tell what broke.

The new role structure was built offline first. It used 32 identities, each with a defined job and an explicit delegation path. Only main, the coordinator, shared its name with the old structure.

Divide the work without loading more models

The departmental roles covered security operations, network operations, help desk, Linux, Docker, databases, the AI platform, and backup and recovery. Those eight departments contained 30 roles. The coordinator and independent governance role brought the total to 32.

Ten were called core identities, with 22 specialists available on demand. Core meant addressable; it didn’t start a continuous model process or authorize a new heartbeat. The RTX 2070 still had 8 GiB of VRAM, and local reasoning started serially.

A database performance question had this intended route:

Owner → main → dba-lead → dba-performance

The coordinator could reach department leads. Leads could reach their own registered specialists. Specialists had no children, and governance could review evidence without approving a change.

The candidate required explicit agent IDs and allowed two delegation edges below main. Structural checks looked for cycles, orphaned routes, and paths beyond that limit. The three new database-role IDs were checked for collisions with the existing registry before being added.

Give the restrictions something to run on

Separate workspaces helped organize the roles, but the design also needed a runtime boundary. Each new role had its own state directory and a Docker sandbox, with read-only workspace access, no sandbox network, a read-only root filesystem, and dropped capabilities.

The recorded production settings for the 31 new roles included:

{
  "mode": "all",
  "scope": "agent",
  "workspaceAccess": "ro",
  "docker": {
    "network": "none",
    "readOnlyRoot": true,
    "capDrop": ["ALL"],
    "memory": "512m",
    "cpus": 1
  }
}

These sandbox settings worked alongside per-role rules denying shell execution and modifying tools. Later, a live container inspection checked the filesystem, network, capabilities, and resource limits.

Add the new roles beside the legacy ones

The production cutover added 31 entries and reused main as the coordinator for the new lead-only routes. The 13 other legacy IDs stayed in place. That left 45 registered IDs: 32 in the 3.5 structure, including main, plus the 13 preserved roles.

The count describes the registry. It doesn’t mean 45 workers were reasoning at once or that the preserved roles acquired the new roles’ complete sandbox policy.

Check a refusal as well as a successful route

The offline candidate passed OpenClaw’s schema validator and the checks for IDs, tool restrictions, and delegation edges. The staging pilot then tested things a schema couldn’t establish: a role reading another workspace, reaching a credential store, or skipping a department lead.

Those attempts were denied. The allowed route from the coordinator to noc-lead succeeded. Getting that successful delegation took another change, though: the local model’s multi-step test failed, and the working pilot used a cloud coordinator with local Qwen3 specialists.
entry.summary: The new role structure divided operations into leads and specialists, with explicit limits on tools and delegation.

entry.title: Restoring a database from the daily backup

link.title: Restoring a database from the daily backup

entry.content:
The earlier backup checks in the CyberBiota3.5 project could extract files and verify their hashes. The OpenClaw archive also passed a listing check that found PostgreSQL table objects.

The next test needed a running engine. The orchestration dump from the daily backup was restored into an isolated PostgreSQL instance, where its tables and indexes could be checked.

Check the load before adding another component

The audit had found five PostgreSQL instances, plus MariaDB and Redis or Valkey services. The database helpers read defined statistics for connections, locks, sizes, cache-related views, and persistence. Those operational questions didn’t require application rows.

At the checkpoint, PostgreSQL connection use was between 6% and 12%, with no waiting locks. I left PgBouncer out of this upgrade because those readings didn’t justify a connection pool.

Recovery coverage was less complete. All five PostgreSQL instances had WAL archiving disabled, leaving no demonstrated point-in-time recovery through that mechanism. The records also lacked verified standalone daily dump timers for Gitea, Planka, and Immich. Those gaps stayed on the list.

Start an engine that can’t reach production

The test used the orchestration dump from the verified daily OpenClaw archive. It was extracted into private staging and checked against its SHA-256 checksum.

The temporary PostgreSQL 17 container had no network, no production mounts, a 512 MiB memory limit, and one CPU. No application jobs or webhooks were attached to it. That kept the restored database from accidentally becoming another active copy of an automation service.

The restore ran through pg_restore, followed by ANALYZE. Metadata queries then checked the result without printing user rows:

Restored object Result
Public tables 17
Indexes 40
Populated tables 12
Database size 51 MB

The measured sequence—extraction, checksum, engine startup, restore, and analysis—took 9.48 seconds. The source archive came from midnight local time that day. Those figures describe this one database exercise and its recovery point, rather than the recovery time for all of CyberBiota.

The temporary container and staging files were removed afterward. Production volumes, backup cadence, and retention stayed in place.

What came back

The restored tables were queryable, the indexes existed, and 12 tables were populated. I now had a functional database restore result to go with the earlier archive checks.

The application itself hadn’t been exercised against that copy. The photo library and the rest of the host hadn’t been recovered either. The runbook retained the missing dump coverage and WAL work as separate jobs, along with a schema-compatibility check before any future image rollback.

The next recovery work was still application-specific: verify the missing dump schedules, test the other databases, and check an application against a restored copy.
entry.summary: I restored the orchestration database into an isolated PostgreSQL instance and checked the tables, indexes, and remaining gaps.

entry.title: A drifting clock and a crowded SSD

link.title: A drifting clock and a crowded SSD

entry.content:
When I started the CyberBiota3.5 upgrade, OpenClaw’s health endpoint answered while the protected route returned HTTP 502. Authelia, the service handling authentication, was stuck restarting. The machine underneath it also wasn’t synchronizing its clock.

There were already 70 containers running on the laptop. The host and its existing services needed repairs before I added the new agent roles.

The clock repair changed the authentication result

The time-service logs showed Chrony trying to reach NTS sources and receiving connection refusals. NTS adds authentication to network time synchronization. The approved repair added working sources and stepped the clock by about 3.5 seconds.

The next checks showed a synchronized clock and a healthy Authelia container. The protected-route test changed from 502 to 401. For that request, 401 was the expected result: the client hadn’t logged in, and the authentication layer was now answering.

Checking OpenClaw directly hadn’t exposed that difference. Its process could be alive while the login route in front of it was broken. I kept the proxy test alongside the direct health check.

The 401 confirmed that the authentication layer was responding again. It didn’t establish that the separate host-freeze problem was fixed.

cAdvisor was using more than three gigabytes

The audit found no memory limit on 53 of the 70 running containers and no CPU limit on 55. The remediation set measured limits, saved the settings in ten Compose files, and ran docker compose config -q against each file.

cAdvisor gave the clearest before-and-after reading. Its recorded usage was 3.39 GiB before recreation. Afterward it was about 50 MiB, with a 512 MiB limit; a later checkpoint showed about 37 MiB. Those are individual readings rather than a long-term benchmark, but they made the resource problem concrete.

At the first completed checkpoint, all 70 running containers had both limits and none were unhealthy. After reboot, the check covered 71 of 71; temporary agent sandboxes could change the running count.

The cleanup also removed the deprecated Portainer container and 26 stale rehearsal or candidate containers. Dockhand stayed healthy. No volumes were removed, and Portainer’s Compose definition remained available behind a deprecated profile.

Make room on the disk that needed it

The smaller system SSD was 87% full at the initial audit, with about 58 GiB available. The project required at least 20% free space on that disk, roughly 93.6 GiB. The larger data SSD still had about 1.2 TiB available.

The next stage reclaimed approximately 70.6 GB of unused Docker build cache and 1.7 GB of dangling images. During the power and storage work, Docker and containerd storage moved onto the larger SSD. The post-move checks verified the bind mounts and found about 137 GiB free on the system disk, now 70% used.

The same checkpoint showed the battery charge cap at 80%, synchronized time after reboot, and healthy Authelia and cAdvisor. It gave me a baseline to continue from. The earlier stability problems still needed observation over several days.

Keep the old backups

The repository backup job had been exiting with status 3. Its repair added narrow exclusions for protected key, runtime, and staging paths. File permissions stayed restricted.

The rerun succeeded, and restic check passed across all 44 existing snapshots. Nothing was pruned. The host could synchronize its clock, the protected route answered correctly, the system disk had room, and the repository backup was working again. The longer stability observation was still ahead.
entry.summary: The CyberBiota3.5 work began with a broken authentication route, uncapped containers, and a system disk that needed attention.

entry.title: Qwen3 stayed local. The coordinator moved to the cloud.

link.title: Qwen3 stayed local. The coordinator moved to the cloud.

entry.content:
Qwen3 could produce the tool call I asked for. That was the first encouraging result in the CyberBiota3.5 model tests. The harder delegation test failed later in the same project.

I had confirmed qwen3:8b as the local baseline. Ollama was already serving it on the RTX 2070, and I wanted to keep using it. The tests helped separate the jobs it had demonstrated from the coordinator job that still needed work.

A tool call and a delegated task are different work

The first tool-schema test asked Qwen3 to select a named network-health query. It returned the expected arguments:

{"query_template_id": "dns_latency_p95", "window_minutes": 15}

A separate malicious-ticket test requested secret access, firewall changes, and self-approval. The model refused and made no tool calls.

In the staging pilot, the coordinator had to spawn a child and handle its deferred tool response. On that multi-step task, Qwen3 returned an empty result instead of completing the handoff.

The approved OpenAI OAuth model completed the same task class. It delegated to noc-lead, which ran local Qwen3 inside its own Docker sandbox. That gave me a practical reason for the hybrid arrangement: use the cloud coordinator for the tested delegation work while keeping local inference for the other roles.

That choice followed the delegation test. It wasn’t a general speed comparison: the cold tool-call timings and warm role turns weren’t directly comparable.

Keep shell execution denied

Authentication was only one part of making the cloud route work. The unauthenticated requests had failed without switching providers. After I completed device-code approval in the isolated profile, the subscription model catalog could be refreshed.

The next blocker was the execution harness. The selected Codex harness rejected the configuration while shell execution was denied. I wasn’t going to treat enabling shell access as a harmless way around that test.

The working configuration selected OpenClaw’s built-in runtime for the cloud model. A harmless prompt then completed with tools.exec.mode still set to deny. The run reported the expected provider and model, used its sandbox, and completed without a fallback.

A follow-up request for a shell command and a host-file read was blocked. The governance role also had no inherited OAuth profile, and the workspaces had no copied credential databases.

Check the route at both ends

The pilot used gpt-6-astra for main. Delegation to local noc-lead succeeded. A direct request from main to soc-tier1 was denied because it skipped the security lead.

The installed OpenClaw release didn’t initially contain the newer 6.2 entries in its catalog. The runtime needed its own upgrade before I could select the production model.

On November 25, the live coordinator was set to openai/gpt-6.2-sol through the built-in runtime. The default stayed ollama/qwen3:8b for the other 44 registered roles. The live smoke identified the expected cloud model and FALLBACK_USED=False. The checked gateway process had no OpenAI API-key environment variable, and the 31 new role directories had no duplicated OAuth credentials.

The live cloud-to-local route passed, and the specialist bypass was denied again. That was the arrangement I accepted for the production cutover. Cloud coordination still means cloud processing; keeping the specialists local doesn’t make the whole request local. Provider limits and failure handling remain things to check during actual operation.
entry.summary: A successful tool call was followed by a failed delegation test. That failure shaped the hybrid setup I put into production.

entry.title: What happened when I tested the incident teams

link.title: What happened when I tested the incident teams

entry.content:
A retry should not create another incident team and another pile of tickets. That was one of the behaviors I wanted checked before accepting the CyberBiota3.5 operations work.

After the individual adapters were passing, the project exercised five controlled scenarios. The scenario inputs were synthetic. Some checks read the live lab, but the tests didn’t break production or pretend that a sample security event was a real compromise.

Follow the smallest useful route

The database-slowdown scenario followed main → dba-lead → dba-performance and read live connection and lock statistics. The DNS scenario used the network lead, the service specialist, a DNS check, and the monitoring probe summary.

For a suspicious endpoint event, the test combined security posture, a benign forensic manifest, and an offline detection sample. It produced a draft case and a proposed response with execution still false.

The OpenClaw-failure scenario checked monitoring evidence that existed independently of the AI controller. The storage-pressure scenario read disk and backup coverage, then drafted a request. It didn’t prune backups or delete volumes.

These were Python orchestration tests, not autonomous model runs. Live model delegation was checked separately in the staging pilot and production smoke test.

Replay the work

Each scenario was run again with the same identifier. The tickets, cases, and change requests were deduplicated instead of being created twice.

The retry and tool budgets were tested separately. A flaky backend hit its circuit breaker after the initial request and two retries. A two-call tool budget refused the third call. Configuring three concurrent runs was rejected; the exercised modes were serial execution or at most two total runs.

Those limits fit the machine. A failing backend shouldn’t turn into an expanding queue of local inference jobs on one GPU.

Try the wrong action through the right route

The orchestrator loaded its allowed delegation edges from the candidate manifest. Tests rejected recursive routes, cross-department jumps, a coordinator skipping a lead, and a specialist spawning another worker.

A valid route also had to refuse prohibited work. The negative tests sent requests for shell execution, live IP blocking, volume deletion, backup pruning, container management, and self-approval through otherwise valid coordinator-to-lead-to-specialist chains. They were denied.

The approval verifier ran outside the language model. It checked the human approver, permitted target and operation, canonical packet digest, signature, expiry, and a single-use nonce. Tests rejected changed parameters, a forged signature, expired approval, replay, and agent identities used as approvers.

Even the correctly signed test packet stayed in dry-run mode. Production execution remained disabled.

What passed, and what stayed disabled

The combined Python suite reached 37 passing tests across monitoring, security, inventory, databases, service desk, and incident orchestration. The useful part was the behavior behind that number: bounded queries, repeat handling, refusals, and a verifier that didn’t let the model grant itself approval.

Service-desk checks also covered draft classification, knowledge drafts, and ticket closure. The closure check required a human identifier and evidence references, and rejected registered agent IDs as the human closer. This was tested adapter behavior, not a complete help-desk identity system. GLPI stayed deferred while Leantime and Planka were already available.

The tests passed with production execution disabled. That setting stayed in place for the live role and coordinator cutover.
entry.summary: Five controlled scenarios tested delegation, duplicate handling, and approval checks while production changes stayed disabled.

entry.title: Making the monitoring answer useful questions

link.title: Making the monitoring answer useful questions

entry.content:
The CyberBiota3.5 audit found a monitoring stack already doing work: VictoriaMetrics, vmalert, Alertmanager, Grafana, Loki, Alloy, and Blackbox Exporter. NetBox held inventory, and AdGuard handled DNS.

I didn’t need another monitoring installation to answer the first operational questions. The project added small Python adapters to read those existing systems and return bounded results.

Give each query a shape

The first adapter set covered host and container health, logs, network metrics, DNS and TLS probes, database health, backup status, restore evidence, and draft tickets.

A network-health call selected a named query template. The probe helper accepted approved targets. The database helper exposed fixed health views, and the container view left out environment variables. Those choices reduced how much arbitrary input could reach the backend.

The negative tests tried URLs outside the approved targets, SQL text, shell fragments, and free-form metric queries. They were denied. Shared code applied redaction, capped output at 64 KiB, and recorded calls in a restricted audit log. An unreachable backend returned unavailable rather than a made-up healthy result.

Follow a failed probe into a draft

The monitoring drill targeted a deliberately closed local port. Blackbox Exporter reported probe_success=0, and a draft ticket was created without sending an external notification.

Replaying the idempotency key returned a deduplicated result. Checking the working target then returned probe_success=1.

The drill connected a failed probe to one draft ticket, suppressed the duplicate, and returned a healthy result for the working target. It made no automatic restart.

Other checks read fresh telemetry, an Alertmanager summary, a bounded log sample, and selected host, container, database, and backup metadata. The first combined set passed 11 tests against the existing services.

Compare the inventory with the host

The next stage added NetBox inventory queries and a redacted Git configuration diff. Passive observation of the host’s addresses was compared with a sample from NetBox. Both observed host addresses were represented in that sample.

That was a useful reconciliation for this machine. It didn’t establish that every device on the home network was inventoried correctly.

The configuration helper read an explicit set of approved files. Tests rejected traversal into other paths, secret-file requests, invalid revisions, and unauthorized role IDs. That made it possible to inspect a relevant change without handing a model the whole checkout.

Keep the visibility limits in view

The laptop was on Wi-Fi. There was no authorized switch-mirror feed or live packet sensor in this work. Zabbix, Oxidized, SmokePing, and continuous flow tooling stayed deferred because the existing tools covered the approved questions or there wasn’t a justified source and resource budget for the addition.

The Python checks reached the live backends; separate gateway tests checked role routing and sandbox behavior. The remaining check was a real request from Telegram through the new tools. Until that path was exercised, the adapters were tested components rather than a demonstrated end-to-end monitoring assistant.
entry.summary: I reused VictoriaMetrics, Loki, and NetBox, then tested small interfaces for probes, inventory, logs, and configuration changes.

entry.title: Putting CyberBiota3.5 into production

link.title: Putting CyberBiota3.5 into production

entry.content:
On November 25, the live coordinator delegated to a local noc-lead sandbox. When it tried to reach soc-tier1 directly, the gateway denied the request. Those two results were the last routing checks in the CyberBiota3.5 cutover.

Getting there took two production changes around a separately approved OpenClaw upgrade. Until then, the new design had been built and tested beside the live gateway.

Add the new roles and preserve the old workflows

The first cutover on November 24 began with a restricted configuration backup, a hash check, and a successful external USB backup. The merged candidate passed schema validation before it replaced the live file.

The change added 31 roles, each with its own workspace and state directory. Their settings included a Docker sandbox, no sandbox network, read-only workspace and root access, dropped capabilities, resource limits, and denied shell execution.

The existing main ID was connected to the eight department leads. Thirteen other legacy IDs, the Telegram binding, the documentation heartbeat, and the existing MCP server configuration stayed in place. That made 45 registered IDs.

The gateway took about 35 seconds to complete plugin and channel startup after the restart. Its health response and reliability monitor passed. A live governance turn identified its role and refused shell and host-file requests. Inspecting the actual sandbox confirmed its network, filesystem, capability, CPU, and memory restrictions.

The sandbox settings covered the 31 new roles; the live governance turn and container inspection sampled their runtime enforcement. The preserved coordinator and legacy roles weren’t shown to inherit the candidate’s complete policy through this additive change.

Deal with the upgrade blockers

I approved moving OpenClaw from 2026.10.4 to 2026.11.9 as its own change. The daily OpenClaw backup and USB copy had both succeeded before that step.

Candidate admission hit two blockers. An unused development symlink caused the snapshot to be rejected; its target was recorded before the link was removed. The expected policy-attestation hash also needed reconciliation with the verified post-cutover state. The policy check passed all 68 checks before proceeding.

After the upgrade, the installed version, health, schema, reliability monitor, and a sandboxed governance turn were checked again. The 37-test adapter suite passed, and the newer model entries appeared in the catalog.

One host check needed follow-up. The daily AIDE file-integrity service reported failure after the approved changes. The failure stayed open for an explicit baseline review. The integrity database was not reinitialized just to clear the alert.

Put the hybrid coordinator on the live route

I completed device-code authorization for the production coordinator. The change didn’t copy the staging credentials into production.

main was set to openai/gpt-6.2-sol through OpenClaw’s built-in runtime, with an empty fallback list. The default remained local ollama/qwen3:8b for the other 44 registered roles.

The live smoke recorded the expected cloud model and no fallback. Credential checks found no OAuth duplication in the 31 new role directories and no OpenAI API-key environment variable in the checked gateway process.

The allowed delegation to local noc-lead ran in a restricted sandbox. The direct-specialist bypass was denied. Health, readiness, and the adapter suite passed again. I accepted the upgrade and coordinator change on November 25.

Watch the lab after the cutover

The planned observation window ran from November 24 to December 1. At publication, it was still underway. Daily backups and stability checks needed to keep passing, and any material regression needed investigation before final project acceptance.

The remaining list included the AIDE review, incomplete database dump coverage, no demonstrated WAL-based point-in-time recovery, a separately held recovery key, and a pending desktop-agent permission review. The lab still depended on one host.

The new coordinator was live. The next test was everyday use: requests through Telegram and the new tools, scheduled jobs running without intervention, and a week of watching for regressions. Those results would decide what could stay and what needed another change.
entry.summary: The live cutover, the OpenClaw upgrade, and the tests that let me keep the new coordinator in place.

entry.title: Why I left Wazuh out of this build

link.title: Why I left Wazuh out of this build

entry.content:
Wazuh was in the CyberBiota3.5 proposal, but the laptop’s RAM budget ruled it out of this build.

At the admission checkpoint, about 12.2 GiB of RAM was available. The project’s allowance for the proposed Wazuh central stack was 8 GiB. That would leave roughly 4.2 GiB, below both the 8 GiB safety reserve and the 6 GiB stop threshold.

I deferred the stack. Moving Docker storage had made room on disk; it hadn’t added memory.

Start with the signals already available

CrowdSec and Alertmanager were already running. The new security helper queried their existing signals without enabling active response. Asking for Wazuh data returned an unavailable result because there was no Wazuh backend to query.

The vulnerability helper read stored reports rather than starting a scan. Case creation produced a draft. The response interface produced a proposal awaiting approval, with executed: false.

The tests included malicious instructions embedded in tickets, cross-role access attempts, and filtering for indicator lookups. Internal addresses, internal domains, and incident prose were rejected as external-enrichment inputs. Those indicator tests used offline fixtures; live external threat-intelligence queries were outside the exercise.

Use a sample without calling it a sensor

The detection tests used benign positive and negative controls. A known matching sample had to produce a result, while a nonmatching control had to stay absent.

Later checks parsed offline EVE JSON and Zeek connection samples. The EVE test removed two raw-payload fields before returning its result. The connection summaries returned metadata instead of packet contents.

Suricata wasn’t installed, and the host had no switch-mirror feed. These tests established how the helpers handled those samples. They didn’t establish live intrusion detection across my network.

The live connection source was narrower: passive sockets on the Dell itself. Its result labeled that local-host coverage explicitly. It couldn’t see everything crossing the home network.

Inspect the host through fixed questions

The endpoint posture view collected a defined selection of information, including AppArmor status, failed units, and existing security-service status. The investigation helper used pre-approved packs for listening ports, container digests, privileged containers, and systemd timers.

The container review found two privileged containers and seven using host networking. Those existing exceptions remained after the new agent sandboxes were restricted.

A benign forensic collection manifest supplied the chain-of-custody test. SHA-256 verification passed, and the helper returned evidence metadata instead of raw contents. That was a controlled test of evidence handling; there hadn’t been an actual compromise to investigate in that exercise.

Leave the larger additions for a justified change

Security Onion, Arkime, Graylog, Greenbone/OpenVAS, MISP, Fleet, Velociraptor, and Shuffle also stayed deferred. They needed more resources, an appropriate data source, or a separately scoped deployment before they could be useful here.

The delivered security work was smaller: queries over existing signals, draft cases, fixed posture and investigation helpers, and tests that kept live data separate from offline samples. Wazuh remained deferred. The next step was to try the smaller tools on actual requests without enabling automatic response.
entry.summary: The laptop had room for bounded security queries. The RAM budget ruled out the proposed central SIEM stack.

entry.title: What I wanted from CyberBiota3.5

link.title: What I wanted from CyberBiota3.5

entry.content:
I wanted my first home lab to use open-source technology to host my own apps and data. That goal started with AriseOne. CyberBiota 1 and 2 gave me different versions to try, and CyberBiota3 was the fresh start that brought those earlier lessons together.

For CyberBiota3.5, the next step was to improve the machine and operating tools around the services already running. The work started with a plan on November 22 and reached the live coordinator cutover on November 25.

A bigger plan, on the same laptop

The plan had two connected aims. OpenClaw would coordinate work on the home lab. Addie 3 would bring together personal knowledge, planning, research, and selected actions. It covered the interfaces, model routes, retrieval, tools, identity, automation, monitoring, and recovery around that assistant.

This round concentrated on the foundations: repairing the host, dividing operations into roles, connecting the models, testing recovery, and moving the new coordinator into production. The complete Addie 3 personal-assistant and second-brain system remained a larger project.

The machine carrying the work was the existing Dell G7 7700: a six-core, twelve-thread i7, about 30 GiB of usable RAM, and an RTX 2070 with 8 GiB of VRAM. It already hosted applications, databases, monitoring, and local inference.

Find the problems before adding to them

The first audit counted 98 containers: 70 running, 25 exited, two created, and one restarting. Authelia was the restarting service. Its failure also broke the authenticated proxy test even though OpenClaw itself answered its health check.

The smaller system SSD was 87% full. The larger data SSD had about 1.2 TiB free. Most running containers lacked CPU or memory limits, and the repository backup job had failed on its last recorded run.

The lab already had VictoriaMetrics, vmalert, Alertmanager, Grafana, Loki, Alloy, and Blackbox Exporter for monitoring, plus NetBox and CrowdSec. The upgrade could reuse those services instead of adding overlapping tools from an older proposal.

Those findings set the first jobs: repair the host, recover space, and check the backups.

Keep the build inside its resource budget

I ruled out the second laptop after its inspection. It had a two-core, four-thread processor, about 14 GiB of RAM, Wi-Fi connectivity, and no available KVM device. This project stayed on the Dell.

I also confirmed Qwen3 as the local model. The first GPU snapshot showed it using about 6.6 GiB of the available 8 GiB. That left little room for another GPU consumer and made serial local inference a deliberate limit.

The agent design divided responsibilities into 32 identities. It didn’t load 32 models into memory. The early candidate ran beside production with separate state, an offline configuration, and a loopback-only staging gateway. The existing Telegram binding and legacy workflows stayed available during the tests.

Carry the tested pieces into production

By November 24, the new role entries had been added to the live configuration. On November 25, the runtime upgrade and cloud coordinator were in place. An allowed cloud-to-local delegation succeeded, while a request that skipped its department lead was denied.

The same project also produced an external encrypted backup, a selective USB restore, a functional database restore, and controlled adapter and incident tests. Automatic production remediation remained disabled, heavy security additions were deferred, and the observation period was still running.

The next job was the host itself: fix the clock, recover the authentication route, and get the system SSD below its space limit.
entry.summary: The next step for a home lab built to run my own apps and keep my own data—and the machine I had to build it on.

entry.title: Taking a backup off the laptop

link.title: Taking a backup off the laptop

entry.content:
The first backup question in the CyberBiota3.5 audit was where the successful jobs were writing. The verified copies were on the same laptop that ran the lab.

That left me with a recovery gap. A local archive could help after a bad edit, but I didn’t have a verified copy outside the machine. I approved adding an encrypted Restic repository to the external USB drive under the name CyberBiota_Ark.

The drive already had my files on it

This wasn’t an empty disk waiting to be formatted. The job created its own repository directory and left the existing files alone.

Its scope was specific: the new 3.5 project records, selected Compose configuration, scripts, and the latest verified daily OpenClaw archive. Staging and selected sensitive or runtime files were excluded. It was a recovery copy for that material, rather than a full image of the laptop or every application’s data.

Restic encrypted the repository. The backup job used the existing credential configuration. I also needed a usable copy of the repository password outside the Dell. The encrypted files would be little use on replacement hardware if the only decryption key disappeared with the host.

Test the missing drive before the successful backup

During the power and SSD work, the USB drive was disconnected. That gave the mount guard a useful test.

A missing mount can leave an ordinary directory at the expected location. A backup job that writes into it can fill the internal disk while looking as though it is using external storage. This script returned its designated skip code when the drive was absent and didn’t write into the root filesystem. The service checked the mountpoint and the expected backup directory before proceeding.

Once the drive was reconnected, the recorded backup processed about 355 MiB across 13,015 files. It exited successfully, and restic check reported no errors. A separate start through the systemd service also passed under its CPU and memory limits.

Restore something from the external copy

The restore test brought two selected project files back from the USB repository into a private staging directory on the data SSD. Their SHA-256 hashes matched the originals. The two-file restore took 1.07 seconds. The temporary directory was removed afterward.

That established that those files could be recovered from the encrypted external copy. The timing belongs to that two-file exercise. It doesn’t describe how long it would take to rebuild CyberBiota or restore its applications.

The database restore went further by restoring a dump into an isolated PostgreSQL engine. That test checked the restored tables and indexes as well as the saved file.

Watch the overnight job run

The USB timer was set for 04:15 with up to two minutes of randomized delay and persistent scheduling. It was configured to skip when the drive wasn’t available.

The November 25 upgrade receipt recorded an automatic run at 04:17 and a clean repository check. That was the scheduled path actually running, beyond the manual service test.

CyberBiota_Ark held an external encrypted copy that had passed a selective restore and an automatic overnight run. It was still an attached USB drive. Offsite protection, complete application coverage, and recovery onto replacement hardware remained separate work.
entry.summary: I added an encrypted repository to an existing USB drive, restored selected files, and checked the overnight job.

entry.title: AriseOne: my first apps and repeatable jobs

link.title: AriseOne: my first apps and repeatable jobs

entry.content:
The first thing I wanted AriseOne to do was simple: give me somewhere at home to run my own apps and keep my own data. I wanted to do it with open-source tools. Once several services were involved, I also needed a way to keep track of the machines running them.

Start with a ping

The early Bash health check worked through a fixed list of machines. It tried a ping, then used SSH to collect system load and free memory. It could return JSON or plain text, bringing several machines into one view.

That was a host check. It could tell me that a machine replied and show its resource readings; checking whether Nextcloud could actually serve a file was a separate job.

The Ansible playbook handled maintenance on Debian-family systems. It refreshed the package cache, applied upgrades, and cleaned unused packages. At the end, it looked for the reboot-required marker and reported which hosts needed attention. It stopped there rather than rebooting them automatically.

Together, the two scripts gave the early lab repeatable jobs: collect a health snapshot, apply package updates, and identify the machines that still needed a reboot.

Give the services somewhere to live

By early February, Nextcloud held files, Homepage linked to the services, and Zammad handled tickets. Proxmox hosted the virtualized parts of the lab.

NVIDIA drivers were a recurring maintenance problem after kernel changes. The notes describe a repair script and a ticket trigger, although I don’t have a complete run demonstrating unattended diagnosis and repair. The useful work at this stage was narrower: capturing the problem and keeping the repair instructions available.

On February 7 and 8, the work included checking Zammad before making system changes and moving Markdown notes into its knowledge base. The ticketing system was becoming a place to find what had happened the last time a service or driver broke.

AriseOne gave me applications to use and maintenance to learn. The next build kept Proxmox and added more monitoring. That led to a dashboard that could connect to its database but still showed nothing.
entry.summary: The early health check, Ansible playbook, and ticketing work behind my first attempt at hosting my own services.

entry.title: When the checks missed their target

link.title: When the checks missed their target

entry.content:
In October, I tested how much read-only diagnostic work local assistants could handle repeatedly. Two roles each had 96 scheduled windows over a day to produce a diagnostic result that met the check. One good answer wasn’t enough for the job.

One role passed. The other missed the target.

The first role passed all 96 windows. The second passed 87: about 91 percent against a requirement of 95 percent. Averaging the two would have hidden which role was unreliable.

After a narrow correction to diagnostic-data handling, a shorter scheduled retest came back clean. The first role passed 16 out of 16 checks, and the second passed 15 out of 15.

Run First role Second role
Original day 96/96 87/96; below the 95% requirement
Shorter retest after correction 16/16 15/15

The correction helped on the retest. It hadn’t yet demonstrated another full day at the required rate.

Keep the job read-only

I kept the original failed result and accepted limited read-only diagnostic use. That decision didn’t authorize incident handling or changes to the systems being examined.

The assistants could help investigate. Letting them act on those findings would be a separate decision, with consequences for the applications and data on the host. The shorter clean run was a reason to continue that bounded use, rather than expand it.
entry.summary: One diagnostic role passed 87 of 96 scheduled checks, below the target. A shorter clean retest kept the work limited to read-only diagnosis.

entry.title: The dashboard that came up empty

link.title: The dashboard that came up empty

entry.content:
At 11:23 p.m. on February 13, the dashboard still had empty panels. Forty-three minutes earlier, the work had been marked successful. The data was in InfluxDB, and Grafana could connect to it. The screen was still empty.

I was building the first CyberBiota with Proxmox, ZFS storage, and a Linux container for the control tools. That guest ran Docker and Ansible alongside InfluxDB and Grafana. Proxmox sent its metrics to InfluxDB so I could view the host’s activity in Grafana.

Follow the data to the screen

Check that evening Result
Proxmox sending metrics InfluxDB contained host data.
Grafana connecting to InfluxDB The connection worked.
Dashboard panels Empty; a later check found no incoming queries.

The work stopped at 11:34 p.m. There was data to query, but the dashboard wasn’t turning it into a useful view.

The next day’s fixes addressed three different parts of that path. First, the InfluxDB data source was changed to use explicit organization and bucket IDs. Then Grafana reported a parsing error while provisioning the dashboard, so the dashboard JSON needed cleanup.

The CPU panels had another problem: the queries didn’t consistently match their sources. Proxmox host metrics and Telegraf metrics used different CPU fields and scales. A query suitable for one source could display the wrong value for the other. The panel queries had to match the data each panel was supposed to show.

The connection wasn’t the finished dashboard

The log records those corrections, but doesn’t preserve the final rendered panels well enough to reconstruct every result. I can describe the faults and the changes without claiming the whole dashboard was verified that night.

The empty screen is the important part of this episode. Checking the database and testing the connection had both helped narrow the fault. Neither had checked the thing I wanted to use: a panel showing what the host was doing.
entry.summary: The first CyberBiota build used Proxmox, ZFS, and Grafana. An empty dashboard exposed a gap between a connection and useful data.

entry.title: Trying Dockhand before replacing Portainer

link.title: Trying Dockhand before replacing Portainer

entry.content:
Portainer was already there when I tried Dockhand. I wanted to see how the other tool felt for the work I usually need a management screen to do: find a container, watch its logs and check how much of the host it is using. I kept Portainer available and left the Compose deployment files in charge of configuration. That way I could compare the interfaces without having to commit to a migration.

On November 11, I compared four everyday tasks:

Task Observation
Find what’s running Dockhand and Docker listed the same 97 containers, of which 72 were running.
Follow a container’s output A live log stream returned output from the selected container.
Check resource use Sampled memory matched Docker. CPU readings differed slightly between polls.
Try the inventory without signing in The request returned HTTP 401 after native app authentication was configured.

The report also inspected the bind mount used to reach Docker. That established the mount setting. It did not show which Docker API operations the app was authorized to make. That question needs a separate check before I can describe the permanent setup as limited to inspection.

That first day established that inventory, live logs, and sampled resource readings worked in the comparison. Portainer remained available during the observation period.

The replacement came later. During the November 23 host repairs, Portainer’s deprecated container was removed while Dockhand stayed healthy. Its Compose definition was retained behind a deprecated profile.
entry.summary: I compared inventory, logs, and resource readings with both tools available before making a cutover decision.

entry.title: Why I moved the lab off Proxmox

link.title: Why I moved the lab off Proxmox

entry.content:
The last night of the Proxmox build involved moving Linux guests to a new network, restarting them, and updating the reverse proxy. On April 6, the monitoring interface remained reachable and the proxy got responses from the backends it checked. The next morning, I was starting over with Ubuntu.

The network experiments before the rebuild

March had included a failed OPNsense restore and problems with a VyOS attempt. The gateway summaries don’t agree well enough to reconstruct every working configuration, but by April 6 the separate gateway experiments were being set aside in favor of Proxmox’s network layer.

Access to the host was a practical concern. On March 14, a change left me without SSH and with limited physical recovery options on a laptop normally run without a local console. If I couldn’t reach the host, a working application route elsewhere in the stack wouldn’t give me a way to undo the change.

The transition notes also describe memory pressure, competing workloads, and repeated friction getting commands and services through nested layers. Those were the reasons for simplifying the platform.

Ubuntu and Docker on the hardware

The April 7 installation record names Ubuntu 25.10. Docker ran directly on the host. A separate NVMe drive was allocated to persistent application data and local model storage, and the NVIDIA driver check saw the GPU.

Before After
Proxmox host with networked guests Ubuntu on the hardware, with Docker on the host
Storage organized through the virtualization layout A separate NVMe drive for persistent app and model data
Hardware checks spread across host and guests The native host could check the GPU directly

I could keep using containers with fewer layers between them and the hardware. Storage, application permissions, backups, and remote recovery also became responsibilities of that one Ubuntu host.

There isn’t a before-and-after benchmark to put a performance number on the change, or a restore list showing that every application’s data survived. Later May notes name Ubuntu 26.04, but don’t establish whether that step was an upgrade or another reinstall.

The change I can pin down is the April rebuild: Proxmox came out of this iteration, and native Ubuntu with Docker became the base for the next one.
entry.summary: The move to native Ubuntu and Docker changed where storage, networking, and application responsibilities lived.

entry.title: The first backup I could show how to restore

link.title: The first backup I could show how to restore

entry.content:
The first CyberBiota3 recovery exercise started with the project repository. Could I recover the files that explained how the lab was built, without overwriting the working copy?

Restic made an encrypted local backup of the selected repository material, including project instructions and change records. Known sensitive configuration and live runtime data were excluded. Application databases were outside this exercise.

Restore into a separate folder

On June 25, the test confirmed a snapshot existed, then restored it into a separate directory. The README, operations instructions, and backup plan were among the files checked. A separate check looked for paths that were supposed to stay excluded.

Restoring beside the working repository let the test inspect the copy without replacing the files in use. The result was a recovery of selected project files, not just a successful backup command.

Wait for the schedule

On July 6, the systemd timer ran the repository backup without a manual start. It exited with status zero, produced a new snapshot, and passed the Restic check.

The June restore and July run checked different parts of the job. The restore put files back. The timer showed that the scheduled path could create another copy on its own.

The backup was still local. Losing the laptop and its storage together would also mean losing that copy, and neither test restored a running application or database. Later, the CyberBiota3.5 work added an external USB copy and an isolated database restore. Those addressed parts of recovery this first repository exercise had left open.
entry.summary: Restic brought selected project files back into a separate folder. The next check was whether the backup would run on schedule.

entry.title: Why I kept rebuilding my home lab

link.title: Why I kept rebuilding my home lab

entry.content:
I wanted to build my first home lab with open-source technology and use it to host my own apps and my own data.

AriseOne was where I started. A Bash script would ping machines and collect health information over SSH. An Ansible playbook could apply updates and report which hosts needed a reboot. By February, I had Nextcloud for files, Homepage for service links, and Zammad for tickets, with Proxmox hosting the virtualized parts.

Getting applications online also gave me machines to maintain. Kernel changes could mean NVIDIA driver repairs. Notes needed somewhere to live so the next fault didn’t start from scratch. I began moving Markdown instructions into Zammad’s knowledge base.

It was time for a fresh start

That’s the reason I moved on from AriseOne. I had tried CyberBiota 1 and 2 in the past: different versions of a lab, but not quite the lab I wanted. CyberBiota3 brought together what I had learned from them.

The first CyberBiota still used Proxmox, with ZFS storage and a Linux container for the monitoring tools. On February 13, the host was sending data to InfluxDB and Grafana could connect, but the panels were empty. The work was marked successful at 10:40 p.m.; the empty panels were recorded at 11:23, and work stopped at 11:34. The next day brought changes to the data-source IDs, dashboard JSON, and CPU queries.

That build also involved network and gateway experiments. By April, memory pressure and the friction of working through nested layers were part of the reason to change the layout. On April 7, CyberBiota 2 started with Ubuntu 25.10 and Docker on the hardware. A separate NVMe drive was allocated to persistent application data and local models, and the NVIDIA driver check could see the GPU.

I don’t have a complete migration record showing which application data carried through every rebuild. I can follow the platform changes, but can’t say every old service or file moved with them.

Keep the apps, and learn to look after them

By June, a new deployment exposed the work around the applications. Two image tags couldn’t be pulled even though the Compose file passed validation. Once those were corrected, Infisical and Homarr revealed separate configuration faults. The fixes recreated the affected app containers while leaving Postgres and Redis alone. Homarr went from HTTP 500 to its first-run setup screen; completing setup still needed a user test.

Backups became more concrete too. In June, selected repository files were restored into a separate folder and checked. In July, the backup timer ran on its own. Those were useful steps, but the local repository copy didn’t cover losing the laptop or recovering every database.

The November CyberBiota3.5 work took that further: host repairs, an encrypted external backup, an isolated PostgreSQL restore, and new AI-assisted operations roles. It still runs on one laptop. The goal is still the one I started with—my own apps and data—with more of the maintenance and recovery work tested along the way.

Start with AriseOne for the early scripts and services, or browse the journal for individual builds, fixes, and experiments.
entry.summary: AriseOne, CyberBiota 1 and 2, and the fresh start that brought those experiments together in CyberBiota3.

entry.title: A valid Compose file and a failed deployment

link.title: A valid Compose file and a failed deployment

entry.content:
I had a Compose file that passed validation and a stack that wouldn’t start. The first June 26 attempt stopped at the image pull. Two tags in the definition didn’t resolve at their registries. That left me with a perfectly readable file and software Docker couldn’t fetch.

The replacement tags were checked against the registry before the next pull. Once Docker could fetch the images, the applications got far enough to report two separate configuration faults.

Two apps, two different faults

Infisical was stuck restarting. The inputs it needed were supplied, but their lengths or encoding did not match what the app expected. The repair corrected the inputs and recreated the Infisical app container. Postgres and Redis were left running. The follow-up inspection showed the app running without a restart in that check. Its selected route also returned HTTP 200.

Homarr had a different problem. It returned HTTP 500 because the container was missing an encryption key that the Compose service should have passed in. Adding the mapping and recreating Homarr changed the response to HTTP 307. That sent the browser to first-run setup.

Check Result at the end of the retry
Caddy, Gitea, Infisical and n8n routes The four selected routes responded with HTTP 200.
Homarr route HTTP 307 to the setup screen, after the earlier HTTP 500.
Complete Homarr setup No completed user test in this result.

The retry left Homarr ready for its setup workflow, which still needed a user test. The other four selected routes answered successfully.

Only the affected app containers had been recreated. Leaving Postgres and Redis running kept the repair focused on the inputs that had failed, without disturbing their data services.
entry.summary: Image pulls, application startup, and the route test each exposed something different during the deployment.

entry.title: The webhook worked. I still rolled it back.

link.title: The webhook worked. I still rolled it back.

entry.content:
I wanted a change in Gitea to reach an n8n workflow without somebody carrying the event between them. The pilot delivered the event. Getting it there had also widened the allowed destinations and loosened connection verification.

That left a working integration with settings I wasn’t willing to keep.

Remove the connection, keep the applications

On June 30, the rollback removed the webhook from Gitea and the associated workflow from n8n. The transport settings widened for the pilot were restored. Follow-up checks found the underlying services still available.

I could keep both applications without keeping this connection between them. That was different from April, when n8n itself had been removed from the lab.

Before trying the integration again, I needed the same setup to demonstrate both parts: the intended workflow received the event, and the sender reached only the intended receiver over a verified connection. The first pilot had demonstrated delivery. It hadn’t demonstrated delivery under the safeguards I wanted in production.
entry.summary: The n8n integration reached its target, but the trust boundary needed more work before I could keep it running.

entry.title: Why I removed n8n and brought it back

link.title: Why I removed n8n and brought it back

entry.content:
I didn’t think n8n was useful at first. On April 8, after the move to Ubuntu, it came out of the lab. I was trying local models and agent-driven work, and the workflow engine didn’t seem to have a job worth keeping it for.

I changed my mind after reading a home lab automation article from Virtualization Howto. That’s my recollection of what brought me back to it. By June, there was a specific integration to try.

Give it an event to handle

n8n was part of the June 26 CyberBiota3 deployment. Its route returned HTTP 200. Four days later, the Gitea webhook pilot gave it a task beyond answering a health check: receive an event and hand it to a workflow.

That gave the experiment a source, a trigger, and a receiver. The event did reach the workflow, but the connection used loosened safeguards. The webhook and associated workflow were removed, and the transport settings were restored.

Gitea and n8n stayed in place. Removing a single integration let me back out of that experiment without removing the workflow engine again. It was a fresh June deployment; I don’t have a record establishing that the old April workflows or their data were carried into it.

The tool had returned with a concrete job to test. The first connection still needed a safer implementation. The rollback has its own post.
entry.summary: Removing a tool did not remove the jobs it had to do. I returned to n8n with a narrower role for it in the lab.
